Galento’s story is one of contradictions: part athlete, part outlaw, part entertainer. He lived fast, fought hard, and left behind a legend as rough and unpredictable as the man himself.

snippet.description:
Briell Decker is a former plural wife of Warren Jeffs, leader of the Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints, or FLDS, a polygamist sect widely considered a cult.

Decker married Jeffs at 18 and spent eight years inside the group while it was being investigated by several law enforcement agencies. Decker explains how the FLDS manipulated its members, including through arranged marriages, financial control, isolation, and the use of religious authority to enforce obedience. She also describes her multiple escape attempts and the pressure the church used to keep members from leaving.

Warren Jeffs was arrested in 2006 and, in 2011, was sentenced to life in prison plus 20 years for sexually assaulting underage girls.

Decker now works with people leaving polygamist communities as founder of the Short Creek Dream Center. She appeared in the HBO Max/Discovery+ documentary "Prisoner of the Prophet."

If you are a survivor of sexual assault, you can call the National Sexual Assault Hotline (1-800-656-4673) or visit its website to receive confidential support.

Dominick “Skinny Dom” Pizzonia, born in 1941 in New York City, was one of the Gambino crime family’s most loyal and enduring members. Raised in the neighborhoods of Queens, he came of age in an era when the Mafia still operated in the shadows — a world where reputation, silence, and relationships meant everything. Starting out as an associate in the 1970s, Pizzonia gradually earned the trust of powerful figures inside the family, including John Gotti and Aniello Dellacroce.

Through decades of internal shifts, federal crackdowns, and leadership changes, Pizzonia remained a steady presence. He served as enforcer, strategist, and decision-maker, commanding respect from crews across Queens and Brooklyn. His reputation wasn’t built on headlines or theatrics — but on discipline, stability, and a deep understanding of the Gambino family’s inner workings.

But even the most loyal soldiers are not immune to the pressures of federal scrutiny. By the 1990s and 2000s, Pizzonia became the focus of major investigations into racketeering and organized crime. Federal cases linked him to extortion, gambling operations, and mob-influenced violence. In the mid-2000s, the government finally delivered a conviction that led to years in federal prison.

Like many longtime members of Cosa Nostra, Pizzonia’s story is a reflection of the Mafia’s transformation — from the glamorous era of Gotti to the quieter, more concealed operations of the modern underworld.
